As for your question, humans have been aware of the existence of outer space for thousands of years. The earliest recorded observations of the night sky date back to ancient civilizations in Mesopotamia, Egypt, and Greece around 4000-5000 years ago. These early cultures believed that the sky was a dome above the Earth and that the stars and planets were gods or spirits.

The concept of a void of darkness in space, illuminated only by stars and galaxies, developed over time through the work of ancient Greek philosophers such as Aristotle and Epicurus. They proposed that the universe was infinite and that the stars and planets were separate from the Earth.

However, it wasn't until the 16th century that the idea of a vast, empty space beyond the Earth's atmosphere began to take shape. The Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus proposed a heliocentric model of the universe, where the Sun was at the center and the planets orbited around it. This idea challenged the geocentric model, which placed the Earth at the center of the universe.

The first person to suggest that space was blue was likely the ancient Greek philosopher Aristotle. In his work "De Caelo" (On the Heavens), Aristotle described the sky as a blue color, which was later adopted by other ancient Greek philosophers.

However, it wasn't until the 19th century that the concept of a blue-colored space became more widely accepted. The French astronomer Urbain Le Verrier proposed that the color of the sky was due to the scattering of sunlight by the Earth's atmosphere, which would eventually lead to the development of modern astrophysics.

The first spacecraft to image the Earth from space was the Soviet Union's Luna 3 mission in 1959. The images showed a blue-colored Earth, which was later confirmed by NASA's Apollo 8 mission in 1968. Since then, numerous spacecraft have imaged the Earth from space, and the concept of a blue-colored space has become a widely accepted fact in modern astrophysics.
